name: Ashok
definition: Ashok is a composite portrait of a Lingayat small-business owner in Mysuru city, drawing together the lived experience of traders and practitioners in the city's established Ayurveda and herbal-products sector. His daily routines, family concerns and civic outlook reflect the perspective of a shopkeeper navigating Mysuru's heritage-tourism economy, managing the balance between traditional medicine's prestige and the pressures of modern retail competition.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Ashok runs a small Ayurveda shop on Sayyaji Rao Road, near the Devaraja Market, selling herbal medicines, oils, powders and consultations for common ailments. He opens at nine each morning, spending the first hour restocking shelves with stock from KSIC depots and local suppliers, then receives a steady stream of customers—elderly regulars seeking arthritis balms, mothers buying kashayams for children's colds, and occasional tourists drawn by Mysuru's sandalwood reputation. He earns between fifteen and twenty-two thousand rupees most months, depending on the Dasara season when footfall surges, though online pharmacies and big-chain stores have begun pulling away younger customers. Afternoons are quieter; he uses the lull to update his GST records on a worn laptop, to call suppliers in Bengaluru, and to advise walk-ins on formulations his father taught him. By six he pulls down the shutters, tallies the day's cash and digital payments, and walks home through the evening market crowds. The work is steady but income growth has stalled; he worries that his sons see the shop as old-fashioned and that rent and stock costs eat into margins each year.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Ashok lives with his wife, Renuka, their two sons—seventeen and fourteen—and his widowed mother in a two-bedroom flat in Vijayanagara, a fifteen-minute scooter ride from the shop. Renuka, trained as a teacher, has not worked outside the home since their elder son was born; she manages the household, cooks, oversees homework and cares for Ashok's mother, who has diabetes and arthritis. Their elder son is in second-year pre-university at a private PU college, preparing for engineering entrance exams; the younger attends a Kannada-medium aided high school nearby. Ashok's father passed away eight years ago, leaving him the shop and its goodwill; his younger brother moved to Bengaluru for a software job and rarely visits. Gender roles in the household are traditional: Ashok handles all financial decisions and shop matters, while Renuka's domain is domestic—though she increasingly questions why their sons do not help with chores. Marriage was arranged by their families; Renuka's father, also a small trader, judged Ashok steady and respectable. The family observes Lingayat customs, wearing vibhuti, visiting the Suttur Mutt during festivals, and contributing to its dasoha meals and school-hostel endowments.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Ashok completed his schooling in Mysuru's government Kannada-medium schools and one year of B.Com at Maharaja's College before his father's illness forced him to take over the shop at twenty-one; he regrets not finishing his degree. His elder son studies at a private PU college charging thirty-five thousand rupees a year; Ashok hopes he will pass the CET and secure an engineering seat, ideally in Mysuru or Bengaluru, though he worries about the cost of private-college fees if the government-quota rank does not come through. The younger son attends a Kannada-medium aided school, performing adequately but showing more interest in cricket than studies. Ashok pays for both sons to attend weekend coaching classes—mathematics and science for the elder, general tuition for the younger—adding another twelve thousand rupees annually. The family debates switching the younger boy to an English-medium school, but Ashok resists the expense and believes Kannada medium builds stronger roots. Renuka wants the boys to study further than their father did, to have salaried stability; Ashok agrees but also hopes one son might take over the shop, blending Ayurveda knowledge with modern marketing. He sees education as the route to security, yet feels his own incomplete degree left him capable enough to run the business his father built.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Ashok's mother attends the K.R. Hospital outpatient diabetes clinic monthly, receiving subsidised insulin and tablets; waits are long, but the care is adequate and cheap. She also suffers from knee arthritis; Ashok treats her with oils and kashayams from his own shop, and occasionally they consult a private Ayurvedic vaidya when her pain worsens. Renuka had a hysterectomy three years ago at a private hospital, costing ninety thousand rupees after insurance; they took a loan from a chit fund to cover the gap. Ashok himself is in fair health—mildly overweight, with occasional acidity—but has not had a full check-up in years; he relies on his own herbal remedies and dismisses the idea of preventive scans as unnecessary expense. The boys are healthy, though the elder suffers exam-season stress and headaches. The family trusts K.R. Hospital and JSS Hospital for serious illness, Ayurvedic treatment for chronic and minor complaints, and private clinics for speed when needed. Ashok worries about the cost of any major health event, knowing his savings are modest and that hospital bills can wipe out years of earnings. His mother's diabetes is managed but not cured; he accepts it as an aging inevitability and focuses on keeping her comfortable.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Ashok's family are practising Lingayats; they wear the ishtalinga, observe veerashaiva customs, and reject caste hierarchy in principle while acknowledging its social weight in practice. They visit the Suttur Mutt during major festivals, contribute to its dasoha free-meal programmes, and sent Ashok's younger brother to a Suttur-affiliated hostel for his high-school years. Ashok respects the Mutt's educational and welfare work and sees it as a unifying institution for Lingayats across Mysuru and Mandya. He also visits the Chamundeshwari Temple during Dasara, participating in the city's shared ritual calendar even though it is not strictly a Lingayat shrine; he sees no contradiction, treating it as part of Mysuru's collective identity. His social circle includes other small traders—some Lingayat, some Vokkaliga, a few Muslim—whom he meets at the market, the trade association and occasional community dinners. Renuka's closest ties are with neighbours and relatives; she attends women's bhajan groups and helps organise Suttur Mutt collection drives in their locality. Ashok values the Lingayat tradition of simplicity and service, but he also navigates Mysuru's broader social fabric pragmatically, maintaining good relations across communities because his shop depends on all customers.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Ashok holds a ration card and his family receives subsidised rice and kerosene, though the PDS shop's irregular hours frustrate him; he buys most provisions from the open market. He opened a Jan Dhan account years ago but uses it rarely, preferring his savings account at Canara Bank. He has not directly benefited from the five guarantees—his household has no woman bus commuter, the electricity subsidy is marginal, and his income sits above the Gruha Jyoti threshold—but he acknowledges that poorer customers mention Shakti and Anna Bhagya as helpful. His shop is registered for GST; he finds the monthly filing cumbersome and pays a small accountant to manage it. He is not a party member but follows politics through Kannada newspapers and evening television news. His encounters with the Mysuru City Corporation are limited to property-tax payment and occasional complaints about road potholes and waste collection; he finds the officials distant and unresponsive. He wishes the government would do more to support small traders against online and chain-store competition, perhaps through lower taxes or dedicated market zones, but he has little faith that his voice reaches decision-makers.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Ashok is proud of Mysuru—the Dasara pageantry, the palace illumination, the city's reputation for order and heritage—and he contrasts it favourably with Bengaluru's chaos and traffic, though he envies Bengaluru's economic dynamism. He worries most about his sons' futures: whether they will secure good college seats, whether they will find stable jobs, and whether they will stay in Mysuru or be pulled to Bengaluru or abroad, leaving him alone in old age. He blames online retail and big pharmacy chains for squeezing small shops like his, and he resents that the government offers them no protection; he feels traditional knowledge and local enterprise are being discarded in the rush toward modern convenience. He is frustrated by the city's slow infrastructure upgrades—potholes, unreliable water supply in some wards, the absence of metro connectivity—and he believes Mysuru is neglected compared with the state's focus on Bengaluru. He respects the Suttur Mutt and the Lingayat community's educational efforts, and he sees his own modest success as the fruit of his father's hard work and his own discipline. He wishes his sons valued the Ayurveda shop as a viable livelihood, not merely a fallback, and he hopes they will remember their roots even if they move away. He demands better support for small businesses, cleaner governance, and recognition that cities like Mysuru deserve as much investment as the capital.
